newsitem.title: USA: Perot loses bid on debates and for more TV time.
newsitem.headline: Perot loses bid on debates and for more TV time.

text.p: Ross Perot suffered a pair of defeats on Friday as a U.S. appeals court refused to include him in the presidential debates and regulators denied his demands for more prime television time for his struggling campaign.
The appeals court rejected a last-ditch, emergency appeal by the Texas billionaire and another third-party presidential candidate over their exclusion from the presidential debates.

Just two days before President Bill Clinton and Republican rival Bob Dole square off in their first debate in Hartford, Conn., the three appellate judges upheld the key parts of a lower-court ruling that rejected Perot's arguments.

Meanwhile, the Federal Communications Commission, by a 4-0 vote, said the big television networks acted legally by refusing to sell the Reform Party candidate extra prime time slots for his half-hour campaign infomercials.
Perot and his running mate, economist Pat Choate, have been stuck at around 5 percent in the polls.

Perot and John Hagelin of the Natural Law Party had sued the Federal Election Commission, a government agency, and a bipartisan commission in an attempt to force their way into the nationally televised debates.

They charged the Commission on Presidential Debates violated Federal Election Commission rules that require "objective" criteria in selecting the debaters and claimed their candidates qualified under rules used since 1988.
The unanimous appeals court upheld all but one minor part of a ruling on Tuesday by U.S. District Judge Thomas Hogan that Perot and Hagelin had failed to prove that their exclusion violated the law.

"In sum, we are unpersuaded that the FEC has unconstitutionally delegated legislative authority to the (debates commission)," the appeals court said in a 16-page ruling that rejected Perot's key argument.
While rejecting Perot's constitutional and legal claims, the appeals court said he could file a new suit challenging the election agency's authority to issue certain regulations.

In his FCC complaint, Perot charged that ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox refused to sell him "reasonable" air time. He alleged that the networks broke a federal law ensuring that candidates have equal opportunity to appear on TV when their opponents appear, and that candidates get "reasonable access" to the airwaves.
He cited, among other elements, the coverage Clinton and Dole received at their parties' nominating conventions in August, plus the air time both will get in the debates.
But the FCC said the networks were exempt from the equal opportunities provision of the law because the Clinton and Dole appearances were "bona fide" news programming.

The agency also said the networks had "properly balanced" Perot's request with their concerns about major programme disruptions. It added that the amount of time the networks offered "satisfied their 'reasonable access' obligations."
Although Perot lost his court case, he plans on Sunday to be on a special edition of CNN's "Larry King Live," right after the debate.
